precepts.text: The mariners cast lots to know for whose cause the evil was upon them, and the lot fell upon Jonah.
precepts.point: When Esther came before the king, he commanded by letters that Haman's wicked device return upon his own head, and that he and his sons be hanged on the gallows.

note.label: Esther 9: Purim and the Victory of the Jews

precepts.why:
Haman “had devised against the Jews to destroy them, and had cast Pur, that is, the lot, to consume them, and to destroy them”. Pur is the lot: the Persian custom of casting lots, and Haman cast it to fix the destruction of Israel.

Casting lots is in the scriptures elsewhere. When the storm came on the ship, the mariners “said every one to his fellow, Come, and let us cast lots, that we may know for whose cause this evil is upon us. So they cast lots, and the lot fell upon Jonah.” The lot was cast to see whose fault the storm was, and it fell on Jonah. That is what a lot is, and Pur is the same thing, cast by Haman to consume the Jews.

But the lot did not decide it. “when Esther came before the king, he commanded by letters that his wicked device, which he devised against the Jews, should return upon his own head, and that he and his sons should be hanged on the gallows.” The lot Haman cast came back on Haman.

precepts.text: The Jews ordained upon themselves and their seed to keep these two days every year throughout every generation, that they should not fail nor the memorial of them perish; this is the Purim being referenced here.
precepts.point: These days in the month Adar, the fourteenth and fifteenth, are kept with assembly, joy, and gladness before the Most High throughout the generations. This is the Feast of Purim referenced back in the canonical account.

note.label: Esther 10: Mardocheus Exalted and the Dream Interpreted

precepts.why:
Mardocheus opens the meaning of his vision. The little fountain that “became a river, and there was light, and the sun, and much water” is Esther, “whom the king married, and made queen”. “And the two dragons are I and Aman.” The nations “were those that were assembled to destroy the name of the Jews”, and his nation is “this Israel, which cried to God, and were saved”. The Most High delivered them from all the evils Aman devised, for Aman was trying to wipe them all out.

He “made two lots, one for the people of God, and another for all the Gentiles”, and “these two lots came at the hour, and time, and day of judgment, before God among all nations. So God remembered his people, and justified his inheritance.” Then the days are set: “in the month Adar, the fourteenth and fifteenth day of the same month, with an assembly, and joy, and with gladness before God, according to the generations for ever among his people.”

Those two days are the Feast of Purim, and the canonical account is where they were ordained. “The Jews ordained, and took upon them, and upon their seed, and upon all such as joined themselves unto them, so as it should not fail, that they would keep these two days according to their writing, and according to their appointed time every year”. They took it upon themselves and upon their seed, every year throughout every generation, that it should not fail nor the memorial of them perish. The fourteenth and fifteenth of Adar kept with assembly, joy and gladness before the Most High are these same two days: the vision of Mardocheus ends at the very feast the canonical book established.

precepts.text: The days were kept as the days wherein the Jews rested from their enemies, and the month turned from sorrow to joy, with feasting and gifts to the poor.
precepts.point: This is the same lesson for our people today. We are going through days of sorrow, but joy is coming as long as we stay in the commandments and trust in the Lord. Search out the former age and the fathers, for this is the story of our people, and it is history to lean on in our own affliction.

note.label: Esther 16: The Second Letter and the Reversal

precepts.why:
The day the chosen people should have perished became a feast. The canonical book names what the feast remembers: “the days wherein the Jews rested from their enemies, and the month which was turned unto them from sorrow to joy, and from mourning into a good day: that they should make them days of feasting and joy, and of sending portions one to another, and gifts to the poor.”

Sorrow to joy, mourning into a good day: that is Almighty God turning the day to joy, kept with feasting, portions sent one to another and gifts to the poor. And it is the same lesson for our people today. We are in days of sorrow, but joy is coming as long as we stay in the commandments and trust in the Lord; the month that turned for them will turn for us.

points: In the twelfth month Adar, on the thirteenth day, when the enemies of the Jews hoped to have power over them, it was turned to the contrary and the Jews had rule over those that hated them.

note.label: Esther 9: Purim and the Victory of the Jews

points: The Jews gathered in their cities, and no man could withstand them, for the fear of them fell upon all people, and the rulers, lieutenants, deputies, and officers helped the Jews because the fear of Mordecai fell upon them.

note.label: Esther 9: Purim and the Victory of the Jews

points: Mordecai was great in the king's house and his fame went throughout all the provinces, and this man waxed greater and greater. Though Esther was queen, she was still subject to Mordecai, the man of Israel who wrote the edict.

note.label: Esther 9: Purim and the Victory of the Jews

points: The Jews smote all their enemies with the sword, slaughter, and destruction, and did what they would to those that hated them.

note.label: Esther 9: Purim and the Victory of the Jews

points: In Shushan the palace they slew and destroyed five hundred men, and they slew the ten sons of Haman the son of Hammedatha, the enemy of the Jews.

note.label: Esther 9: Purim and the Victory of the Jews

points: On the spoil they laid not their hands.

note.label: Esther 9: Purim and the Victory of the Jews

points: The number slain in Shushan was brought before the king, who told Esther the Jews had slain five hundred men and the ten sons of Haman, and asked what more she desired.

note.label: Esther 9: Purim and the Victory of the Jews

points: Esther asked that the Jews in Shushan be granted the next day also according to the decree, and that Haman's ten sons be hanged on the gallows.

note.label: Esther 9: Purim and the Victory of the Jews

points: The king commanded it done, and the Jews in Shushan gathered on the fourteenth day and slew three hundred more, but on the spoil they laid not their hands.

note.label: Esther 9: Purim and the Victory of the Jews

points: The other Jews in the king's provinces gathered, stood for their lives, had rest from their enemies, and slew of their foes seventy and five thousand, laying not their hands on the prey.

note.label: Esther 9: Purim and the Victory of the Jews

points: This was on the thirteenth day of Adar, and on the fourteenth they rested and made a day of feasting and gladness.

note.label: Esther 9: Purim and the Victory of the Jews

points: The Jews of Shushan rested on the fifteenth day, so the Jews of the unwalled towns made the fourteenth a day of gladness, feasting, and sending portions one to another. This is where the gift giving of Purim comes from.

note.label: Esther 9: Purim and the Victory of the Jews

points: Mordecai wrote these things and sent letters to all the Jews near and far to establish that they keep the fourteenth and fifteenth days of Adar yearly.

note.label: Esther 9: Purim and the Victory of the Jews

points: These were the days the Jews rested from their enemies, the month turned from sorrow to joy and from mourning to a good day.

They were to make them days of feasting, joy, sending portions one to another, and gifts to the poor. This is where the feast of Purim comes from, a feast that commemorates the destruction of Israel's enemies.

note.label: Esther 9: Purim and the Victory of the Jews

points: The Jews undertook to keep what Mordecai wrote, because Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite had devised against the Jews to destroy them and had cast Pur, that is the lot, to consume them.
Pur was the Persian custom of casting lots, much like the lot cast for Jonah to see whose fault the storm was.

note.label: Esther 9: Purim and the Victory of the Jews

points: When Esther came before the king, he commanded by letters that Haman's wicked device return upon his own head, and that he and his sons be hanged on the gallows.

note.label: Esther 9: Purim and the Victory of the Jews

points: These days were called Purim after the name Pur, and the Jews ordained and took upon themselves and their seed to keep these two days every year.

note.label: Esther 9: Purim and the Victory of the Jews

points: The days were to be remembered and kept throughout every generation, family, province, and city.
These days of Purim should not fail from among the Jews nor the memorial of them perish from their seed, which shows Israel still celebrates Purim today.

note.label: Esther 9: Purim and the Victory of the Jews

points: Esther the queen, the daughter of Abihail, and Mordecai the Jew wrote with all authority to confirm this second letter of Purim.

note.label: Esther 9: Purim and the Victory of the Jews

points: Letters were sent to all the Jews in the hundred twenty and seven provinces with words of peace and truth, to confirm the days of Purim in their appointed times.

note.label: Esther 9: Purim and the Victory of the Jews

points: The decree of Esther confirmed these matters of Purim, and it was written in the book, which is Israel's own book of history.
